monument_name: Sera stone inscription of Ripu Malla (early 14th century)
description_en: The inscription dates from an early 14th century and is inscribed on the south façade of a stone boulder, located in a field of the hamlet of Sera. Sera is accessible via tracks that wind through fields from Sahubada.This is an important historical record because it mentions Ripu Malla, a Khaśa Malla king who reigned between at least 1312 CE and 1316 CE (Andolfatto 2019). Despite his seemingly short rule, Ripu Malla was a very active ruler. He inscribed his name on the Ashokan pillars at Nigliva and Lumbini. In 1313 CE, he also visited the Kathmandu Valley. During the visit, he was able to attend the ritual bathing of Buṅgadyaḥ in Bungamati, as well as visit Svayambhu and Pashupatinath.During one of his travels, Ripu Malla most likely had the opportunity to commission apaubhā(now in the collection ofAlain Bordier in Switzerland) depicting him and his son worshipping a white Tārā. A gilt copper statue of Ḍākinī Nairātmā (now at theLos Angeles County Museum of Art, inv. no. M.85.221) with Ripu Malla's name cast at the base is another work of art bearing his mark (Andolfatto 2022).Ripu Malla's inscriptions in Nigliva and Lumbini both begin with the mantra 'oṃ maṇi padme huṃ' written in Tibetan or in Nāgarī scripts. This is also true of the Sera inscription. The mantra 'oṃ maṇi padme huṃ' precedes the name 'Ripu Malla' in the text.  Four lines in Nāgarī script follow this. Yogi Naraharinath first mentioned the inscription in 1956 CE (Naraharinath 1956: p. 80). No date could be identified in the inscription.
